passage:
Monday: After their fight about his job move, Nitin went silent. Jahnavi followed him from the kitchen to the balcony. "Talk to me! Why do you always do this?" He put on his headphones and went for a walk. She sent nine messages. No reply till midnight.
Thursday: At the next disagreement, she tried something different. "I can see you're shutting down. I need us to finish this. Can we pick it up on Sunday evening, after dinner?" He blinked, then nodded.
Sunday: At eight he came to the table, a bit stiff, and talked for twenty minutes. When he began drifting off again, Jahnavi said calmly, "It's okay to pause. It's not okay to vanish for days. That's my limit." He sat back down.

qa.q: How many messages did Jahnavi send on Monday?
What was Jahnavi feeling on Monday when she followed Nitin, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt shut out and desperate; she followed him from room to room and asked why he always does this.

qa.q: What changed on Thursday, and why did it work better?
qa.a: She calmly named his shutting down and asked to continue at a set time, which gave him space without dropping her need.

qa.q: How might Nitin experience a calm request compared with being chased?
qa.a: Being chased probably made him feel cornered, so he left; a calm, timed request felt manageable, so he came back.

grounding: Over a week, a woman whose partner goes quiet in conflict moves from chasing him to calm, direct requests and a clear personal limit.

passage: Come, sit with your old Sarita ammachi. When I married your grandfather Thomas, I was twenty-five and he was a closed box. Any quarrel, he would walk out to the church compound and sit there for hours. I used to run after him, crying, pulling his sleeve, and he only went further, to the fish market, anywhere. One evening my own mother said, "You are chasing a cat. Sit still and tell him plainly." So the next time, I said, "Thomas, when you leave in the middle, I feel alone. Come back in one hour and we'll finish." Then I made my tea and did not follow. He came back in forty minutes. It took years, but he learned to stay. And I learned to stop running.

qa.q: Where would Thomas go after a quarrel?
qa.a: He would walk out to the church compound and sit there for hours.

qa.q: What did Sarita feel when Thomas left in the middle of a quarrel?
qa.a: She felt alone and upset, which is why she used to run after him crying.

qa.q: What was the turning point in how Sarita handled quarrels?
qa.a: She told Thomas plainly how she felt, asked him to come back in one hour and stopped following him.

qa.q: How might Thomas have felt when Sarita stopped chasing him?
qa.a: He probably felt less cornered, which made it easier to return on his own; he came back in forty minutes.

grounding: A grandmother recalls feeling shut out by a husband who left during quarrels, and how calm, plain requests worked better than chasing.
